slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study The Midnight Visitor by Robert Arthur, a short spy story in which an unarmed man defeats an armed one. Please read the story in your textbook, Footprints without Feet, before you go on. This lesson does not repeat the text. The board tests this reader through short and long answers, so that is our focus.

slides.heading: How to use this lesson
bullets: Read the story once in *Footprints without Feet*.
Use these slides for the sequence of events, the themes and the characters.
The board asks 3-mark and 6-mark questions on this reader, not extracts: practise those most.
Explain events **in your own words**; do not memorise lines.
slides.narration: Here is how to use this lesson. Read the story first. Then use these slides for the order of events, the themes and the four characters. The board does not print extracts from this reader; it asks short and long answers. So practise explaining, in your own words, how Ausable sets his trap and why it works.

slides.narration: Robert Arthur, who lived from nineteen hundred and nine to nineteen sixty-nine, was an American writer of mystery and suspense. He wrote radio mysteries and created the Three Investigators books for young readers. This is a short spy story with a twist ending. It is told in the third person, mostly following Fowler, a young writer who watches everything happen.

slides.heading: The story in six stages
slides.body_md: From disappointment to astonishment in one evening. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

visual.alt: Flow of the story in six stages: a disappointing spy; a gun in the room; the balcony story; a knock at the door; a scream below; and only the waiter.
visual.caption: The story in six stages (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The story moves through six stages. Fowler is disappointed by an ordinary-looking spy. They find a man with a gun in the room. Ausable tells a story about a balcony. There is a knock at the door. A scream rises from below. And the visitor turns out to be only the waiter. Keep this map in mind as we go.

slides.heading: Summary 1: a disappointing spy
slides.body_md: Fowler, a young writer, hopes to see the thrilling world of a secret agent. Instead he follows Ausable, a fat, untidy man, to an ordinary hotel room. Ausable even suggests that the work is mostly dull. Fowler is disappointed.
slides.narration: Fowler is a young writer who has dreamed of meeting a real secret agent. He expects glamour and excitement. Instead he follows Ausable, a fat, untidy man, up to an ordinary hotel room, and Ausable even suggests that his work is mostly dull. Fowler is disappointed, and so, at first, is the reader. That is exactly what the writer intends.

slides.heading: Summary 2: a gun in the room
slides.body_md: When the light goes on, a man named Max is waiting with a pistol. He is a rival agent and wants a report about new missiles that Ausable expects that night. Fowler is thrilled and frightened; Ausable stays calm, almost irritated.
slides.narration: When the light goes on, everything changes. A man called Max is waiting in the room, holding a pistol. He is a rival agent, and he wants a report about new missiles that Ausable is expecting that night. Fowler is thrilled and frightened at the same time. Ausable, however, stays calm, as if Max were only a nuisance.

slides.heading: Check: the order of events
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events from the story are shuffled. Put them in order, from Fowler’s disappointment to the arrival of the waiter.

slides.heading: Summary 3: the balcony story
slides.body_md: Ausable grumbles that intruders keep getting into his room by a balcony outside his window, and says he has complained to the hotel. Max believes him. There is no balcony; Ausable has invented it.
slides.narration: Now Ausable begins his trap. He grumbles, almost to himself, that intruders keep getting into his room by a balcony outside his window, and that he has already complained to the hotel. Max believes every word. But there is no balcony at all. Ausable has made it up on the spot, mentioning it so casually that it sounds like a dull, everyday fact.

slides.heading: Summary 4: the knock and the scream
slides.body_md: A knock comes at the door. Ausable says it must be the police, whom he had asked to check on him. Frightened, Max decides to hide on the balcony and climbs over the sill. A scream rises from the street below.
slides.narration: Then there is a knock at the door. Ausable says it must be the police, whom he had asked to check on him because of the report. Max cannot risk meeting the police, so he decides to hide on the balcony until they leave. He climbs over the window sill, and a moment later a scream rises from the street far below.

slides.heading: Summary 5: only the waiter
slides.body_md: The door opens. It is Henry, a waiter, bringing the drinks Ausable had ordered. Ausable had known who would knock and used it in his trap. Fowler is astonished.
slides.narration: Finally the door opens, and it is not the police at all. It is Henry, a waiter, bringing the drinks that Ausable had ordered. Now we understand: Ausable knew all along who would knock, and he used that ordinary visit to frighten Max. Fowler is astonished. The dull-looking man has won a deadly contest without lifting a finger.

slides.heading: Theme 1: appearance versus reality
slides.body_md: Nothing in the room is quite what it seems.
columns:
**What seems true**

- Ausable is a dull, ordinary man
- Max, with a gun, is in control
- there is a balcony
- the police are at the door

**What is true**

- Ausable is a brilliant agent
- Ausable is in control
- there is no balcony
- it is only the waiter
slides.narration: The central theme is appearance versus reality. Ausable seems dull, but he is brilliant. Max, with his gun, seems in control, but Ausable is. There seems to be a balcony, but there is none. And the knock seems to be the police, but it is the waiter. In answers, show how each false appearance leads to the surprise.

slides.heading: A web of themes

rows: A dull-looking man is a brilliant agent; the balcony is not there.
Ausable thinks clearly with a gun pointed at him.
An unarmed man defeats an armed one.
Fowler’s fantasy against Ausable’s plain routine.
The knock, the scream, the waiter.

visual.alt: Table of six themes with where each appears: appearance versus reality, presence of mind, brains over force, romance versus reality of spying, overconfidence, and suspense and surprise.

slides.narration: Around that theme sit others. Presence of mind, as Ausable thinks clearly at gunpoint. Brains over force, since the unarmed man wins. The romance of spying against its reality. Max’s overconfidence, which makes him underestimate his opponent. And the craft of suspense and surprise, built through the knock, the scream and the waiter’s arrival.

slides.heading: Check: the quiet winner
slides.narration: Check yourself. In a quiz final, a quiet student who looks nervous beats the confident favourite by staying calm. Which character in the story does the quiet student resemble?

slides.heading: Character: Ausable, looks and mind
slides.body_md: Your syllabus asks you to contrast his appearance with his intelligence.

rows: Calm and steady under a gun
Lives in an ordinary hotel room
A quick inventor of convincing stories
A careful planner who uses an expected knock

visual.alt: Table contrasting how Ausable looks, fat, untidy, ordinary and unheroic, with what he is: calm, inventive, a careful planner who wins without a weapon.

slides.narration: Ausable looks fat, untidy and ordinary, and he lives in a plain hotel room. Nothing about him suggests a hero. But his mind is calm, inventive and careful. He keeps steady under a gun, makes up a convincing story, and uses an expected knock as part of his plan. He wins without a weapon. That contrast is the heart of the story.

slides.heading: Fowler, Max and Henry

rows: A young writer with romantic ideas of spying; the observer whose reactions mirror ours
Armed and confident, but gullible and quick to panic
The waiter whose ordinary knock becomes part of the trap

visual.alt: Table of the other characters: Fowler, a young writer and observer; Max, armed and confident but gullible and panicky; Henry, the waiter whose knock becomes part of the trap.

slides.narration: Fowler is a young writer with romantic ideas of spying. He is the observer, and his disappointment and astonishment mirror ours. Max is armed and confident, but gullible and quick to panic, which proves fatal. Henry, the waiter, does almost nothing, yet his ordinary knock becomes the key to Ausable’s trap.

slides.heading: Why the unarmed man wins
columns:
**Max’s mistakes**

- trusts his gun, not his judgement
- underestimates a plain-looking man
- believes a casual remark
- panics at the word police

**Ausable’s strengths**

- stays calm
- invents a believable detail
- plans around an expected knock
- lets his enemy defeat himself
slides.narration: Why does the unarmed man win? Max trusts his gun instead of his judgement, underestimates a plain-looking man, believes a casual remark and panics at the word police. Ausable stays calm, invents a believable detail, plans around a knock he expects, and lets his enemy defeat himself. Use these contrasts in long answers.

slides.heading: Check: why Max fell
slides.narration: Try this assertion and reason item. Decide whether each statement is true, and then whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Suspense and the twist
bullets: **Anticlimax first:** a dull opening lowers our expectations.
**Sudden danger:** a gun in a small room.
**Mystery:** why is Ausable talking about a balcony?
**Pressure:** the knock forces a quick decision.
**Twist:** the feared police are only a waiter, and everything makes sense.
slides.narration: How does Arthur build suspense? He begins with an anticlimax, so we expect nothing. Then comes sudden danger: a gun in a small room. Ausable’s talk of a balcony adds mystery. The knock adds pressure. And the twist, when the waiter walks in, makes us look back and see how every detail fitted the plan.

slides.heading: Appearance and reality: SOYL’s own examples
slides.body_md: Practise spotting how a story can use a false appearance. These sentences are SOYL’s own, not from the story:
bullets: *The new boy in the torn sweater quietly solved the puzzle that had beaten the whole class.* — a plain appearance hiding ability
*The guard dog that frightened every visitor turned out to be scared of the cat.* — a fierce appearance hiding weakness
*The locked box the thieves fought over held only old school reports.* — a prize that is not what it seems
slides.narration: Here are three sentences of our own. A boy in a torn sweater solves the puzzle: a plain appearance hiding ability. A fierce guard dog fears the cat: a fierce appearance hiding weakness. A box of old reports: a prize that is not what it seems. Now find how Arthur uses appearance and reality in your textbook.

slides.heading: Word meanings

rows: a person who enters without permission
the ability to think and act quickly in a crisis
anxious uncertainty about what will happen
an unexpected turn in a story

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: intruder, gullible, composure, deceptive, presence of mind, suspense, twist and espionage.
visual.caption: Key words for this story with their meanings.

slides.narration: These words will help you write about the story. An intruder enters without permission. Gullible means easily tricked. Composure is calmness under pressure. Deceptive means giving a false impression. Presence of mind is the ability to think and act quickly in a crisis. Suspense is anxious uncertainty, a twist is an unexpected turn, and espionage is the work of spies.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a 6-mark answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* *Appearances can be deceptive.* Discuss with reference to the story.
bullets: **Stand:** agree; nothing in the story is what it seems.
**Points + evidence:** Fowler misjudges Ausable; Max underestimates him; the balcony and the police are inventions.
**Turn:** the waiter’s arrival reveals the truth.
**Value + conclusion:** judge people by their qualities, not their looks.

Give points with evidence: Fowler misjudges Ausable, Max underestimates him, and the balcony and the police are both inventions. Then show the turn, when the waiter’s arrival reveals the truth. Finish with a value: judge people by their qualities, not their looks.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Fowler expects a glamorous spy and is disappointed by fat, untidy Ausable.
Max waits in the room with a pistol, after a report on new missiles.
Ausable invents a balcony and says the knock is the police.
Max climbs out to hide and falls; the visitor is Henry, the waiter.
Read the story in *Footprints without Feet*; write about it in your own words.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Fowler expects a glamorous spy and meets fat, untidy Ausable. Max is waiting with a pistol for a report on new missiles. Ausable invents a balcony and says the knock is the police. Max climbs out to hide and falls, and the visitor is only the waiter. Read the story in your textbook and write in your own words.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: 3-mark answers (40–50 words): point + evidence + explanation.
6-mark answers (100–120 words): stand → 3 points with evidence → value or theme → conclusion.
Facts often confused: the balcony never existed; the knock was the waiter, not the police; Ausable used no weapon.
For character questions, contrast Ausable’s looks with his actions.
Value questions: presence of mind, calm under pressure, not judging by appearances.
slides.narration: Exam tips. In three mark answers, give a point, evidence and a short explanation. In six mark answers, take a stand, give three supported points, and link to a value. Get the facts right: the balcony never existed, the knock was the waiter, and Ausable used no weapon. And in character answers, contrast his looks with his actions.

sections.body_md:
**Read the story itself in your textbook, *Footprints without Feet* (NCERT supplementary reader).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the text.

**Robert Arthur** (1909–1969) was an American writer of mystery and suspense, known for radio mysteries and the *Three Investigators* series. This is a short spy story with a twist ending, told in the third person and mostly seen through the eyes of Fowler, a young writer.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL’s words)
sections.body_md:
**The disappointment.** Fowler, a young writer, hopes to see the thrilling life of a secret agent, but Ausable is fat and untidy, his hotel room is ordinary, and he calls the work dull.

**The intruder.** In the room, Max, a rival agent, waits with a pistol for a report about new missiles that Ausable expects that night. Ausable stays calm.

**The trap.** Ausable grumbles about a balcony outside his window that lets intruders in. Max believes him; there is no balcony.

**The knock.** Ausable says the knock must be the police. Max decides to hide on the balcony, climbs over the sill, and a scream is heard from below.

**The twist.** The visitor is Henry, a waiter, with drinks Ausable had ordered. Fowler is astonished.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Appearance versus reality:** Ausable, the balcony and the knock are all different from how they seem.
- **Presence of mind:** clear thinking at gunpoint.
- **Brains over force:** the unarmed man wins.
- **Romance versus reality of spying:** Fowler’s fantasy against Ausable’s routine.
- **Overconfidence:** Max underestimates his opponent.
- **Suspense and surprise:** the knock, the scream, the waiter.

**Message:** intelligence and calm matter more than looks or weapons; never judge by appearances.

key_terms.definition_md: The ability to think clearly and act wisely in a sudden crisis.

sections.heading: 8. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**How this reader is examined:** the board sets 3-mark short answers (40–50 words; two of three) and a 6-mark long answer (100–120 words) on *Footprints without Feet*. It does not print extracts from this reader; SOYL’s commentary items are comprehension practice only.

**Short answers (3 marks):** point + evidence + explanation.

**Long answers (6 marks):** a clear stand; three points with evidence in your own words; a link to a value or theme; a one-line conclusion. Extrapolation tasks (Fowler’s diary, Ausable’s report to his chief) must stay consistent with the story.

Re-read the story in *Footprints without Feet* before a test.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** Footprints short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words, two of three) and one long answer (6 marks, 100–120 words) (CBSE 2026-27, Section C). No extracts from this reader.

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant events, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view or value), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Saying there was a balcony: Ausable invented it.
2. Saying the police arrived: it was Henry, the waiter.
3. Saying Ausable fought or shot Max: he used no weapon.
4. Treating Fowler as the hero: he is the observer.
5. Quoting lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the story in your textbook, *Footprints without Feet*.

questions.solution_md: Parts (a)–(c) recall the opening; (d) and (e) interpret its purpose.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) a writer

**(b)** (d) Ausable looked fat and ordinary, not like a glamorous spy.

**(c)** glamour

**(d)** So that Ausable’s later cleverness comes as a surprise, proving that looks can mislead.

**(e)** (a) Appearances can be deceptive.

questions.passage_md: Arthur begins by puncturing a fantasy. Fowler, a young writer, has longed to meet a real secret agent, and he has imagined glamour: beautiful strangers, coded whispers, gunfire in the night. Instead he is led by Ausable, a heavy, untidy man who looks nothing like the hero of a spy film, up to an ordinary hotel room high in the building. Ausable himself seems to agree that the work is mostly dull, a matter of papers and waiting. The reader shares Fowler's disappointment, which is exactly what the writer wants, because the story is about to prove that appearances can be badly misleading.

questions.passage_md: The moment the light goes on, the dull evening changes. A man named Max is waiting inside Ausable's room, and he is holding a pistol. He is another agent, and he has come for a report about new missiles that Ausable is expecting to receive that night. Fowler is thrilled and frightened at once: here, at last, is the drama he wanted. Ausable, by contrast, shows almost no surprise. He speaks to the intruder calmly, even with mild irritation, as if Max were a nuisance rather than a threat. That calm is the first real sign that this unimpressive man is more formidable than he looks.

questions.stem_md: In *The Midnight Visitor*, the fat, untidy secret agent is called ___.
questions.solution_md: The agent is **Ausable**.

questions.stem_md: The waiter who knocked at Ausable’s door was named ___.
questions.solution_md: The waiter was **Henry**.

questions.stem_md: The armed intruder, ___, had come for a report about new ___.
questions.solution_md: **Max** wanted the report on new **missiles**.

questions.stem_md: The surprise arrival of the waiter gives *The Midnight Visitor* a ___ ending.
questions.solution_md: It has a **twist** ending.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ausable remained calm when he found Max in his room.

**Reason (R):** Ausable’s calm manner made his story about the balcony believable.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R describes an effect of his calm, not the reason he was calm.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Max fell when he climbed out of the window.

**Reason (R):** There was no balcony outside Ausable’s window.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The police knocked at Ausable’s door at the end of the story.

**Reason (R):** Henry, the waiter, brought the drinks Ausable had ordered.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: it was the waiter, not the police. R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fowler was disappointed when he first met Ausable.

**Reason (R):** Fowler had once worked as a secret agent himself.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: Fowler was a young writer, not an agent.

questions.stem_md: True or false: in *The Midnight Visitor*, Ausable looked exactly like a glamorous film spy.
questions.solution_md: **False.** He was fat and untidy.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Ausable defeated Max without using any weapon.
questions.solution_md: **True.** He used only words and quick thinking.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the balcony Ausable described was real.
questions.solution_md: **False.** He invented it.

questions.stem_md: True or false: Max wanted a report concerning new missiles.
questions.solution_md: **True.** That was the paper he came for.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of *The Midnight Visitor* in the order in which they happen.

options.text_md: Henry the waiter enters with drinks.
Max is found waiting in the room with a pistol.
Max climbs out of the window.
Fowler is disappointed by Ausable’s appearance.
There is a knock at the door.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (d) → (a). Disappointment → Max → the balcony → the knock → the fall → the waiter.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of Ausable’s trap in *The Midnight Visitor*.

options.text_md: He claims the knock is the police.
Ausable stays calm before the pistol.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Calm → the invented balcony → the false police → Max’s choice → the fall.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)
